name: Laser genesis
lead: Laser Genesis is the name of a non-ablative skin treatment that uses a long-pulsed 1064-nm neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet (Nd:YAG) laser at low energy. People have it to improve overall skin tone, reduce visible redness and soften fine lines, and it is described by providers as a gentle option with little downtime. A split-face trial refers to it as the 1064-nm long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser known as Laser Genesis.[1]

The Nd:YAG laser medium emits infrared light at 1064 nm, which is weakly absorbed by water-rich tissue and is used in medicine for hair removal, minor vascular lesions and other dermatologic applications.[2] The first working Nd:YAG laser was demonstrated in 1964 at Bell Laboratories.[2]

Published evidence specific to Laser Genesis for appearance consists of one randomized split-face study that compared it with grid fractional radiofrequency for periorbital wrinkles in eight patients,[1] plus several small registered studies of 1064-nm devices.[3][4] The same 'Laser Genesis' technique has also been reported for toenail fungus in a Japanese clinical paper, which describes a 5 mm spot, sequential low-fluence irradiation and a showering-like motion.[7]

paras: Nd:YAG lasers are solid-state lasers whose main output is invisible infrared light at 1064 nm. Because the wavelength is poorly absorbed by water, it can reach beneath the skin surface, and the same laser type is used for hair removal, small facial or leg vessels and other procedures [2].

Clinics that offer Laser Genesis describe delivering repeated low-energy pulses to warm the dermis without damaging the surface, with the aim of changing the look of redness, pore size and fine lines. Registered studies of other 1064-nm non-ablative devices have addressed photoaging and pigmentation [4].

The Genesis name originates with Cutera, whose laser platforms carry settings such as Laser Genesis and Green Genesis; registered trials refer to a Cutera Excel V laser with a Green Genesis setting.[3] Unlike ablative lasers, non-ablative treatments leave the epidermis intact, which is why providers describe minimal downtime.

A randomized, single-blind, split-face prospective study in Filipino patients (eight participants with moderate to severe periorbital wrinkles) compared grid fractional monopolar radiofrequency with the 1064-nm Laser Genesis. Its authors noted that controlled head-to-head comparisons of the two had been lacking [1].

Several small studies registered on ClinicalTrials.gov have tested Cutera-type Genesis or 1064-nm devices. These include a 17-person open-label study of 1064 nm for non-ablative rejuvenation in photoaging and pigmentation [4], a 20-person evaluation of a Cutera Excel V laser with a Green Genesis setting for wrinkles, rosacea and scarring [3], a 9-person study of a non-ablative laser for brow-lift scars [5], and a 100-patient chart review of a GenesisPlus laser for toenail fungus [6]. Registry entries do not by themselves report outcomes.

The toenail-fungus report used the Laser Genesis technique in refractory onychomycosis and assessed nail turbidity scores on a five-point scale, illustrating the broader use of the same handpiece settings outside facial rejuvenation.[7]

The Nd:YAG literature notes eye injury as the principal hazard of 1064-nm lasers because the beam is invisible [2]. Specific adverse-event rates for Laser Genesis in cosmetic use have not been reported.

Laser Genesis is offered under that brand name in dermatology and aesthetic clinics, and is often presented as a lunchtime treatment given in a course of sessions. Related 1064-nm Nd:YAG devices are widely used for hair removal and vascular lesions.[2] It is not a prominent topic in looksmaxxing forums, where users more often discuss fractional and ablative lasers.

card.summary: A gentle 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser facial treatment marketed for tone and redness; published appearance evidence is very thin.
card.note: Evidence specific to this brand consists of one eight-patient split-face trial and small registered studies.

quick.overview:
Laser Genesis is a brand name for a low-energy 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser treatment that clinics offer for skin tone, redness and fine lines, usually described as having little downtime.
Published research on it for appearance is sparse. One randomized split-face trial in eight people compared it with fractional radiofrequency, and other registered studies are small.
quick.mechanism: The infrared light passes through the surface and warms the dermis without removing the epidermis; providers say this prompts collagen remodeling and less visible redness.
quick.risks: Nd:YAG lasers at 1064 nm carry an eye-injury hazard because the beam is invisible. Cosmetic adverse-event rates for this specific treatment have not been reported.

chain: Low-energy 1064-nm pulses warm the dermis without removing the surface
Providers say this reduces visible redness and prompts collagen remodeling
Clinic-described result: more even tone and softer fine lines
angle.text: Clients book a series of short sessions to even out skin tone, calm redness and refine texture with little recovery time. Results are described by providers as gradual and temporary.
